content: 1. Deaths among patients diagnosed with visceral leishmaniasis (VL) can occur due to various causes, including VL itself, HIV, other diseases or medical conditions, serious adverse events, non-medical conditions, or unknown causes. All deaths should be documented with the specific cause identified. 2. Loss to follow-up refers to patients who fail to return for assessment after completing treatment or whose status is not recorded. 3. At the final assessment, treatment outcomes are categorized as follows: Final cure: A patient remains symptom-free for six months after completing treatment. Relapse: Recurrence of VL symptoms with parasitological confirmation at any time after initial cure. Death: Any death occurring in a patient diagnosed with VL, regardless of treatment status or cause, within the standard post-treatment follow-up period. 4. After completing treatment, patients may be discharged if they show clinical improvement, have been screened and managed for comorbid conditions, secondary infections, and complications, and have received nutritional supplementation. 5. Before discharge, patients should receive counseling about the disease, its treatment, potential medication side effects, signs of opportunistic infections, and symptoms that require medical consultation. Essential information should be documented on treatment cards, with a copy provided to the patient. 6. Most patients are referred to specialized centers for care. Providing information about closer referral centers can help conserve resources. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) has highlighted the need for a biomarker to confirm post-chemotherapeutic cure and improve monitoring and disease control. Currently, parasitological confirmation is the standard method for assessing treatment response. 8. HIV co-infected patients are at higher risk of VL relapse, necessitating critical follow-up to detect recurrence and provide timely management. Follow-up should occur at six-month intervals or as per national protocols, with adjustments for clinical indications or migratory patients. 9. Relapse of VL is defined as the recurrence of symptoms with parasitological confirmation after initial cure. Risk factors for relapse include previous VL episodes, low CD4 counts (<200/mm³), failure to achieve cure after the first episode, lack of ART initiation, and absence of secondary prophylaxis. 10. Treatment for relapse may involve repeating the same regimen or using alternative drugs. Extended therapy is recommended if there is no good clinical response after the first course. Rescue treatment is considered for cases of treatment failure or non-response. 11. Secondary prophylaxis can be initiated after achieving a test of cure. In East Africa, trials have shown multiple relapses during follow-up periods, with treatments including combination regimens, liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB), and sodium stibogluconate. Antimonials, due to their toxicity, require careful monitoring for pancreatitis and cardiotoxicity. 12. In cases of multiple relapses or non-responsiveness, clinicians should consider compassionate treatment options while being mindful of the risk of drug resistance. Palliative care may be necessary for patients with incurable VL and associated complications. 13. WHO defines palliative care as the prevention and relief of suffering for patients and families facing life-threatening illnesses, addressing physical, mental, social, and spiritual needs. 14. Pregnant women with VL face significant risks, including spontaneous abortion, small-for-gestational-age newborns, and congenital leishmaniasis. Treatment decisions should weigh the benefits against potential risks to the mother and fetus. Liposomal amphotericin B is preferred for treating VL during pregnancy, while miltefosine is contraindicated due to its teratogenic effects. 15. Children and the elderly have limited data on combination therapy for VL. Liposomal amphotericin B is the safest option across all age groups, with specific dosing recommendations based on age and weight. 16. HIV testing should be offered to all populations in high-burden settings and to specific groups in low-burden settings, including those with clinical signs of HIV, HIV-exposed children, and pregnant women. Community-based testing and self-testing are recommended to improve access and linkage to care. 17. HIV testing algorithms should achieve at least 99% positive predictive value, with a combination of tests ensuring high sensitivity and specificity. Retesting is recommended before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) to confirm HIV status. 18. ART should be initiated rapidly for all individuals living with HIV after confirmed diagnosis and clinical assessment, ideally within seven days.
